parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 4. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man asking a friend for advice about organising a surprise birthday party. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Chloe: Hi, Ben. You said you wanted to ask me something? Ben: Yes, have you got a few minutes? It's about my sister, Rachel. She turns thirty next month, and I want to throw her a surprise party. You organised one for your husband last year, didn't you? Chloe: I did, and it went really well, actually. Nobody gave the secret away. What do you want to know? Ben: Well, first of all, where to have it. My flat's far too small, and I don't really want to hire a big hall. Chloe: No, a hall can feel a bit empty unless you've got a hundred guests. We used the upstairs room at a pub called the Fenwick Arms. Ben: The Fenwick Arms? How do you spell that? Chloe: F, E, N, W, I, C, K. It's on Mill Street, just behind the cinema. Ben: Oh, I think I know it. Is the room big enough for about forty people? Chloe: Easily. It holds about sixty, and it has its own bar, so nobody has to keep going downstairs. Ben: And what does it cost to hire? Chloe: When we booked it, it was a hundred and fifty pounds for the evening. But I was talking to the manager a few weeks ago, and he said they've put it up to a hundred and eighty. Ben: Hmm. That's still reasonable, especially if it's for the whole evening. Chloe: It is. And you don't pay anything extra for the sound system or the tables. Ben: What about food? Did the pub do that for you? Chloe: They offered, but their menu is mainly burgers, and we wanted something a bit nicer. We thought about ordering pizzas, but then people would have been eating out of boxes all evening. In the end, we ordered a buffet from Rossi's, that Italian deli on the high street. They delivered everything and even collected the plates the next day. Ben: That sounds ideal. Were they expensive? Chloe: Not really. About twelve pounds a head. One thing, though. Make sure you tell them if anyone has allergies. They need to know when you place the order, because they prepare some dishes separately. Ben: Right. Actually, one of Rachel's friends can't eat nuts, so I'll need to mention that. Chloe: And what about a cake? Rachel will expect a cake, even if the party is a surprise. Ben: Of course. Where did you get yours? Chloe: From Crumbs, the bakery near the station. The cake was amazing, but you have to plan ahead. Their website says you need to order a week before, but when I rang them, they said for anything with decorations, it's ten days. Ben: Ten days. OK, I'll get on to that soon. And music? I don't know whether to get a DJ or just put a playlist together. Chloe: Well, DJs are pretty expensive. There's an old piano in the upstairs room, but it hasn't been tuned for years, so I wouldn't rely on that. What we did was book a saxophone player for the first hour, while people were arriving. Everyone loved it. Ben: Oh, that's a lovely idea. Rachel's always liked jazz. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Ben: What about decorations? Did you do much? Chloe: Not a lot. The room already looks quite nice. We were going to put up banners with his name on them, but the party shop had sold out, so we just got loads of balloons, in silver and gold. They looked great. Ben: Balloons. That's easy enough. Now, the part I'm most worried about is keeping it a secret. How did you invite people? Chloe: Well, whatever you do, don't set up a group on social media. That's how most surprises get spoiled, because someone always posts something by mistake. I sent everyone an email, with a warning not to reply to all in capital letters at the top. Ben: Good idea. Rachel checks her phone constantly, so I'll avoid anything she might see. What time did you ask the guests to arrive? Chloe: We originally said eight o'clock, but then we realised my husband might turn up early, so we changed it to seven thirty. You want everyone there at least half an hour before the guest of honour. Ben: Makes sense. And how did you get your husband there without him guessing? Chloe: I told him we were meeting two old friends for a quiet drink. He had no idea. Ben: I'll think of something similar. Did anyone take photos on the night? Chloe: Yes, I asked a friend who's good with a camera to take pictures all evening, so I didn't have to worry about it. Afterwards, we put all the photos into an online album, so everyone who came could look at them and download their favourites. Ben: That's a nice touch. Rachel would love that. Chloe: And one more piece of advice. Relax and enjoy yourself on the night. Nothing ever goes exactly to plan. Ben: I'll try. Thanks so much, Chloe. That's been really helpful. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a cycling museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hartley Cycle Museum. My name's Megan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we begin, I'd like to give you some practical information, and then I'll tell you a little about the history of the bicycle, which is what our main gallery is all about. Guide: I can see quite a few families here today, so first, a few words for parents. In the main hall, you'll see several copies of early bicycles. Children are welcome to sit on them and have their photos taken, but please don't let them try to ride them, as they're very easy to fall off. Downstairs, there's a workshop where our volunteers restore old bikes. There are a lot of sharp tools down there, so children must stay with an adult the whole time they're in that area. Guide: We normally give out activity sheets for children at reception, but I'm afraid we've run out today. However, every child who visits today can enter our prize draw. Just fill in a card at the entrance to the cafe, and we'll pick a winner at four o'clock. The prize is a family ticket for our summer festival. Guide: Now, a few words about what's new. Many of you will have visited us before, and you may remember the short film about the history of cycle racing. That's still showing every hour in our small cinema, and it's as popular as ever. This year, though, we've introduced an audio guide, which you can download onto your phone free of charge using the code on your ticket. It's only in English at the moment, but we're hoping to add other languages next year. Guide: The other new feature this year is our repair demonstrations. Twice a day, at eleven and at three, one of our mechanics shows visitors how to fix a puncture and adjust their brakes, and you're welcome to ask questions. We had also hoped to open a cycle track for families in the garden this summer, but unfortunately that won't be ready until next spring. And some of you may have heard talk of a rooftop cafe, but I'm afraid that's still only an idea. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Right, let's move into the main gallery, which tells the story of the bicycle. The machine in this first case looks a little like a bicycle, but you'll notice it has no pedals at all. It was designed in eighteen seventeen by a German inventor, Karl Drais. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet on the ground, rather like a child's balance bike today. It was sometimes called a running machine, and for a short time it was very fashionable. Guide: It took several decades before anyone thought of attaching pedals to the front wheel, and it's not clear exactly who did it first, because several people claimed the idea. What we do know is that in eighteen sixty-eight, the first recorded bicycle race took place, in a park just outside Paris. It was only about twelve hundred metres long, and it was won by a young Englishman. Cycling clubs began to appear in many countries soon after that, although historians disagree about which one was the very first. Guide: The next case contains a high-wheeler, or penny-farthing, as it was later called. The enormous front wheel meant that riders could travel faster, but they sat so high up that a small stone in the road could throw them over the handlebars. That's why the machine in the next case, which appeared in eighteen eighty-five, was such a breakthrough. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that drove the back wheel, so the rider sat much lower down. In fact, it was known as the safety bicycle, and its basic shape is the one we still use today. Guide: Even so, riding was still uncomfortable, because the wheels had solid rubber tyres. Then, in eighteen eighty-eight, a Scottish vet living in Ireland, John Boyd Dunlop, developed a tyre filled with air, originally for his young son's tricycle. Interestingly, someone else had patented a similar idea more than forty years earlier, but it had never caught on. Dunlop's tyre, on the other hand, was soon being used everywhere. Guide: With safe, comfortable machines available, cycling became hugely popular, especially among women, for whom it offered a new kind of freedom. Bicycles with a lower frame were produced so that women could ride in long skirts, although we don't know the exact date of the first one. And in nineteen oh three, a French sports newspaper organised a race that took riders on a route around the whole of France. That was the very first Tour de France, and of course it's still held every summer. Guide: The last case in this section contains a set of gears. For many years, the organisers of the Tour de France refused to let riders use gears, because they believed the race should test the strength of the rider, not the quality of the machine. It wasn't until nineteen thirty-seven that riders in the race were finally allowed to use gears that could be changed while riding. OK, if you'd like to follow me through to the next gallery. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Jack and Priya, discussing an assignment on outdoor learning in primary schools. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Priya: How's your part of the assignment going, Jack? Jack: Slowly, but I've found some really interesting research. I hadn't realised how many different benefits there are when children have lessons outdoors. Priya: I knew about some of them. Obviously, they get more exercise, so their fitness improves. That's hardly news. Jack: No, I'd have expected that too. But I had no idea that time outdoors could protect children's eyesight. There's quite strong evidence that children who spend more time outside are less likely to become short-sighted. Priya: Yes, that surprised me as well. I'd always thought short sight was mainly something you inherited from your parents. Jack: And what about teamwork? Several studies found that children cooperated better on outdoor tasks. Priya: That seems fairly predictable to me, though. If they're building a shelter or something, they have to work together. Jack: I suppose so. I was more surprised by the language results. Priya: Me too. I'd never have guessed that children would use a wider range of words outside, but apparently they talk much more when they're describing things they can touch and see. Jack: Exactly. And then there's the research on stress levels. I found that quite unexpected. Priya: Really? I read a lot about that for my psychology module last year, so it wasn't new to me at all. Jack: OK. Then there's the section on problems. Teachers mention bad weather more than anything else. Priya: But that's the easiest thing to deal with, surely. If the children have waterproof clothing and boots, there's no reason not to go out. And the school can keep a few sets for children who don't have their own. Jack: True. Safety is much harder, though. Some parents get very anxious about their children climbing trees or using tools, and it takes a long time to change those attitudes. Priya: Yes, I'm not sure there's a quick solution to that. And cost can be a real issue for some schools. Even simple equipment adds up. Jack: Although lots of activities don't need any equipment at all. Priya: That's true, but schools still worry about it. What about children getting overexcited? Some teachers say it's hard to get them to settle once they're outside. Jack: I think that's quite easy to fix, actually. If you set up a clear routine, like always meeting at the same spot and using a signal to get their attention, they soon calm down. Priya: I agree. That just needs a bit of planning. Lack of space is more difficult. Some city schools only have a small yard. Jack: Yes, and you can't just create a field out of nowhere. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Jack: I tried some outdoor maths during my teaching placement. I was worried the children wouldn't concentrate, but they were fine, and it didn't take much preparation either. What struck me was that when they measured real trees and paths instead of lines in a textbook, they really understood what the numbers meant. Priya: That's a great example to include. One thing I found tricky was assessment. There's often no written work to mark. Jack: Some teachers get the children to assess each other, don't they? Priya: Yes, but I'm not convinced that works with young children. I think the best approach is to take photos of what the children produce, like a pattern made of leaves, and keep them as a record of how their skills develop over the year. Jack: Good idea. I was also reading interviews with head teachers. Quite a few of them like the idea of outdoor learning, but their main concern is test results. They're under a lot of pressure, and they think time outside will take time away from preparing for tests. Priya: Yes. Funding came up too, but less often than you'd expect, and hardly anyone mentioned parents. Jack: Do you think outdoor learning will become more common? Priya: Well, I can't see the government making it compulsory. It has too many other priorities. Jack: No, I don't think it'll be compulsory either. But I'm sure universities will start including it in teacher training. At the moment, most new teachers have never been shown how to teach outside, and that's bound to change. Priya: I hope so. What worries me most is children who've grown up in big cities. Some of them have hardly ever been to a wood or a field, and they can be quite frightened at first, of insects, or of getting dirty. Jack: But schools usually provide boots and coats, don't they? Priya: Yes, clothing isn't really the problem. It's more about helping them feel comfortable in a new environment. Jack: Did you do much outdoor learning at primary school yourself? Priya: Not much. But we had one teacher, Mr Hughes, who took us out to the woods every Friday, whatever the weather. I'm still really thankful to him. I remember everything we did there. Jack: It's funny, I had a teacher like that too. She's probably the reason I want to teach. I feel very grateful that she made the effort. Priya: We should mention that in the introduction. Shall we meet again on Thursday to put it all together? Jack: Sounds good. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about bats and rice farming in Thailand. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Good morning. Over the last few weeks, we've been looking at ecosystem services, that is, the benefits that people receive from wild species, often without realising it. Today I'd like to focus on a group of animals with a rather poor reputation: bats. Bats are often associated with darkness and disease, and many people find them frightening. But for farming communities living near their roosts, they can be extremely valuable neighbours, as I hope to show you today. I'll be drawing on a research project I took part in recently in a rice-growing province of central Thailand, where several large colonies of bats roost in limestone caves close to farmland. Lecturer: Most people in the area are small-scale rice farmers, and the bats bring them a surprising number of benefits. The species we studied feed at night on flying insects, and a large colony can eat several tonnes of them in a single night. People often assume that bats mainly eat mosquitoes, but we found relatively few of those. When we examined the bats' droppings, we found the remains of moths in large quantities, as well as planthoppers, tiny insects that can destroy entire rice fields. By reducing the numbers of these pests, the bats save farmers a great deal of money that would otherwise be spent on chemicals. Lecturer: The droppings themselves are valuable too. They're known as guano, and local people collect them from the cave floors and sell them. In the past, guano was also used to make gunpowder, but today it's used almost entirely as a fertiliser, because it's so rich in nutrients. Farmers told us it gave better results than anything they could buy in a shop. Lecturer: Other species of bat feed on nectar rather than insects, and they're important pollinators. It's sometimes said that mangoes depend on bats, but in fact they're mainly pollinated by insects. The durian, on the other hand, is a very good example. Its flowers open at night, and bats are its main pollinators, so without them, farmers would harvest far less of this valuable fruit. Lecturer: In recent years, the bats have also brought income of another kind. Every evening, just at dusk, millions of bats pour out of the caves in long, twisting streams, and this spectacle now attracts large numbers of tourists, who spend money in local restaurants and guesthouses. The bats return at dawn, but very few visitors get up early enough to see that. Lecturer: However, despite these benefits, bat numbers in the region appear to be falling, and our project looked at the reasons. Over two years, we interviewed more than two hundred households and also counted the bats leaving several caves at regular intervals. One important cause is disturbance in the caves. Guano collection is a valuable source of income, but when collectors enter the caves during the breeding season, mothers may abandon or drop their young. The authorities have tried to ban collection during those months, but the rules aren't always followed. Lecturer: Bats are also hunted in some areas. Before we started, I'd assumed they were caught mainly for use in traditional medicine, but the people we spoke to told us it was for their meat, which is sold at local markets. That's a concern for human health as well, as bats can carry viruses. Lecturer: Loss of roosting sites is another problem. Some species roost in temples, where they're generally left alone. But others live in hollow trees, and as old trees have been cut down to make way for farmland and roads, these bats have lost their homes. And finally, noise from traffic seemed to make little difference to the bats, but we found that bright lighting near cave entrances, from new roads and tourist facilities, delayed their emergence in the evening, which meant they had less time to feed. Lecturer: So what can be done? We considered planting more trees, but that would take decades to have any effect. Instead, we tested the installation of bat boxes. These are small wooden shelters fixed to poles near the rice fields, and within a year, around half of them were being used. We also found that bats were more numerous on farms where farmers had reduced the amount of pesticides they used. These chemicals not only kill the insects that bats feed on, but may also poison the bats themselves. Persuading farmers to change their habits isn't easy, of course, so in the second part of the lecture, I'll look at how we tried to do that. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Questions 15-20

Which event in the history of the bicycle took place in each of the following years?

Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-H, next to Questions 15-20.

Events
A   the invention of tyres filled with air
B   the founding of the first cycling club
C   permission to use gears in a major race
D   a machine with no pedals
E   the first bicycle designed for women
F   the first recorded race for cyclists
G   a race around an entire country
H   a design that made cycling much safer

parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 4. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man asking a friend for advice about organising a surprise birthday party. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Chloe: Hi, Ben. You said you wanted to ask me something? Ben: Yes, have you got a few minutes? It's about my sister, Rachel. She turns thirty next month, and I want to throw her a surprise party. You organised one for your husband last year, didn't you? Chloe: I did, and it went really well, actually. Nobody gave the secret away. What do you want to know? Ben: Well, first of all, where to have it. My flat's far too small, and I don't really want to hire a big hall. Chloe: No, a hall can feel a bit empty unless you've got a hundred guests. We used the upstairs room at a pub called the Fenwick Arms. Ben: The Fenwick Arms? How do you spell that? Chloe: F, E, N, W, I, C, K. It's on Mill Street, just behind the cinema. Ben: Oh, I think I know it. Is the room big enough for about forty people? Chloe: Easily. It holds about sixty, and it has its own bar, so nobody has to keep going downstairs. Ben: And what does it cost to hire? Chloe: When we booked it, it was a hundred and fifty pounds for the evening. But I was talking to the manager a few weeks ago, and he said they've put it up to a hundred and eighty. Ben: Hmm. That's still reasonable, especially if it's for the whole evening. Chloe: It is. And you don't pay anything extra for the sound system or the tables. Ben: What about food? Did the pub do that for you? Chloe: They offered, but their menu is mainly burgers, and we wanted something a bit nicer. We thought about ordering pizzas, but then people would have been eating out of boxes all evening. In the end, we ordered a buffet from Rossi's, that Italian deli on the high street. They delivered everything and even collected the plates the next day. Ben: That sounds ideal. Were they expensive? Chloe: Not really. About twelve pounds a head. One thing, though. Make sure you tell them if anyone has allergies. They need to know when you place the order, because they prepare some dishes separately. Ben: Right. Actually, one of Rachel's friends can't eat nuts, so I'll need to mention that. Chloe: And what about a cake? Rachel will expect a cake, even if the party is a surprise. Ben: Of course. Where did you get yours? Chloe: From Crumbs, the bakery near the station. The cake was amazing, but you have to plan ahead. Their website says you need to order a week before, but when I rang them, they said for anything with decorations, it's ten days. Ben: Ten days. OK, I'll get on to that soon. And music? I don't know whether to get a DJ or just put a playlist together. Chloe: Well, DJs are pretty expensive. There's an old piano in the upstairs room, but it hasn't been tuned for years, so I wouldn't rely on that. What we did was book a saxophone player for the first hour, while people were arriving. Everyone loved it. Ben: Oh, that's a lovely idea. Rachel's always liked jazz. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Ben: What about decorations? Did you do much? Chloe: Not a lot. The room already looks quite nice. We were going to put up banners with his name on them, but the party shop had sold out, so we just got loads of balloons, in silver and gold. They looked great. Ben: Balloons. That's easy enough. Now, the part I'm most worried about is keeping it a secret. How did you invite people? Chloe: Well, whatever you do, don't set up a group on social media. That's how most surprises get spoiled, because someone always posts something by mistake. I sent everyone an email, with a warning not to reply to all in capital letters at the top. Ben: Good idea. Rachel checks her phone constantly, so I'll avoid anything she might see. What time did you ask the guests to arrive? Chloe: We originally said eight o'clock, but then we realised my husband might turn up early, so we changed it to seven thirty. You want everyone there at least half an hour before the guest of honour. Ben: Makes sense. And how did you get your husband there without him guessing? Chloe: I told him we were meeting two old friends for a quiet drink. He had no idea. Ben: I'll think of something similar. Did anyone take photos on the night? Chloe: Yes, I asked a friend who's good with a camera to take pictures all evening, so I didn't have to worry about it. Afterwards, we put all the photos into an online album, so everyone who came could look at them and download their favourites. Ben: That's a nice touch. Rachel would love that. Chloe: And one more piece of advice. Relax and enjoy yourself on the night. Nothing ever goes exactly to plan. Ben: I'll try. Thanks so much, Chloe. That's been really helpful. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a cycling museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hartley Cycle Museum. My name's Megan, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we begin, I'd like to give you some practical information, and then I'll tell you a little about the history of the bicycle, which is what our main gallery is all about. Guide: I can see quite a few families here today, so first, a few words for parents. In the main hall, you'll see several copies of early bicycles. Children are welcome to sit on them and have their photos taken, but please don't let them try to ride them, as they're very easy to fall off. Downstairs, there's a workshop where our volunteers restore old bikes. There are a lot of sharp tools down there, so children must stay with an adult the whole time they're in that area. Guide: We normally give out activity sheets for children at reception, but I'm afraid we've run out today. However, every child who visits today can enter our prize draw. Just fill in a card at the entrance to the cafe, and we'll pick a winner at four o'clock. The prize is a family ticket for our summer festival. Guide: Now, a few words about what's new. Many of you will have visited us before, and you may remember the short film about the history of cycle racing. That's still showing every hour in our small cinema, and it's as popular as ever. This year, though, we've introduced an audio guide, which you can download onto your phone free of charge using the code on your ticket. It's only in English at the moment, but we're hoping to add other languages next year. Guide: The other new feature this year is our repair demonstrations. Twice a day, at eleven and at three, one of our mechanics shows visitors how to fix a puncture and adjust their brakes, and you're welcome to ask questions. We had also hoped to open a cycle track for families in the garden this summer, but unfortunately that won't be ready until next spring. And some of you may have heard talk of a rooftop cafe, but I'm afraid that's still only an idea. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Right, let's move into the main gallery, which tells the story of the bicycle. The machine in this first case looks a little like a bicycle, but you'll notice it has no pedals at all. It was designed in eighteen seventeen by a German inventor, Karl Drais. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet on the ground, rather like a child's balance bike today. It was sometimes called a running machine, and for a short time it was very fashionable. Guide: It took several decades before anyone thought of attaching pedals to the front wheel, and it's not clear exactly who did it first, because several people claimed the idea. What we do know is that in eighteen sixty-eight, the first recorded bicycle race took place, in a park just outside Paris. It was only about twelve hundred metres long, and it was won by a young Englishman. Cycling clubs began to appear in many countries soon after that, although historians disagree about which one was the very first. Guide: The next case contains a high-wheeler, or penny-farthing, as it was later called. The enormous front wheel meant that riders could travel faster, but they sat so high up that a small stone in the road could throw them over the handlebars. That's why the machine in the next case, which appeared in eighteen eighty-five, was such a breakthrough. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that drove the back wheel, so the rider sat much lower down. In fact, it was known as the safety bicycle, and its basic shape is the one we still use today. Guide: Even so, riding was still uncomfortable, because the wheels had solid rubber tyres. Then, in eighteen eighty-eight, a Scottish vet living in Ireland, John Boyd Dunlop, developed a tyre filled with air, originally for his young son's tricycle. Interestingly, someone else had patented a similar idea more than forty years earlier, but it had never caught on. Dunlop's tyre, on the other hand, was soon being used everywhere. Guide: With safe, comfortable machines available, cycling became hugely popular, especially among women, for whom it offered a new kind of freedom. Bicycles with a lower frame were produced so that women could ride in long skirts, although we don't know the exact date of the first one. And in nineteen oh three, a French sports newspaper organised a race that took riders on a route around the whole of France. That was the very first Tour de France, and of course it's still held every summer. Guide: The last case in this section contains a set of gears. For many years, the organisers of the Tour de France refused to let riders use gears, because they believed the race should test the strength of the rider, not the quality of the machine. It wasn't until nineteen thirty-seven that riders in the race were finally allowed to use gears that could be changed while riding. OK, if you'd like to follow me through to the next gallery. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Jack and Priya, discussing an assignment on outdoor learning in primary schools. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Priya: How's your part of the assignment going, Jack? Jack: Slowly, but I've found some really interesting research. I hadn't realised how many different benefits there are when children have lessons outdoors. Priya: I knew about some of them. Obviously, they get more exercise, so their fitness improves. That's hardly news. Jack: No, I'd have expected that too. But I had no idea that time outdoors could protect children's eyesight. There's quite strong evidence that children who spend more time outside are less likely to become short-sighted. Priya: Yes, that surprised me as well. I'd always thought short sight was mainly something you inherited from your parents. Jack: And what about teamwork? Several studies found that children cooperated better on outdoor tasks. Priya: That seems fairly predictable to me, though. If they're building a shelter or something, they have to work together. Jack: I suppose so. I was more surprised by the language results. Priya: Me too. I'd never have guessed that children would use a wider range of words outside, but apparently they talk much more when they're describing things they can touch and see. Jack: Exactly. And then there's the research on stress levels. I found that quite unexpected. Priya: Really? I read a lot about that for my psychology module last year, so it wasn't new to me at all. Jack: OK. Then there's the section on problems. Teachers mention bad weather more than anything else. Priya: But that's the easiest thing to deal with, surely. If the children have waterproof clothing and boots, there's no reason not to go out. And the school can keep a few sets for children who don't have their own. Jack: True. Safety is much harder, though. Some parents get very anxious about their children climbing trees or using tools, and it takes a long time to change those attitudes. Priya: Yes, I'm not sure there's a quick solution to that. And cost can be a real issue for some schools. Even simple equipment adds up. Jack: Although lots of activities don't need any equipment at all. Priya: That's true, but schools still worry about it. What about children getting overexcited? Some teachers say it's hard to get them to settle once they're outside. Jack: I think that's quite easy to fix, actually. If you set up a clear routine, like always meeting at the same spot and using a signal to get their attention, they soon calm down. Priya: I agree. That just needs a bit of planning. Lack of space is more difficult. Some city schools only have a small yard. Jack: Yes, and you can't just create a field out of nowhere. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Jack: I tried some outdoor maths during my teaching placement. I was worried the children wouldn't concentrate, but they were fine, and it didn't take much preparation either. What struck me was that when they measured real trees and paths instead of lines in a textbook, they really understood what the numbers meant. Priya: That's a great example to include. One thing I found tricky was assessment. There's often no written work to mark. Jack: Some teachers get the children to assess each other, don't they? Priya: Yes, but I'm not convinced that works with young children. I think the best approach is to take photos of what the children produce, like a pattern made of leaves, and keep them as a record of how their skills develop over the year. Jack: Good idea. I was also reading interviews with head teachers. Quite a few of them like the idea of outdoor learning, but their main concern is test results. They're under a lot of pressure, and they think time outside will take time away from preparing for tests. Priya: Yes. Funding came up too, but less often than you'd expect, and hardly anyone mentioned parents. Jack: Do you think outdoor learning will become more common? Priya: Well, I can't see the government making it compulsory. It has too many other priorities. Jack: No, I don't think it'll be compulsory either. But I'm sure universities will start including it in teacher training. At the moment, most new teachers have never been shown how to teach outside, and that's bound to change. Priya: I hope so. What worries me most is children who've grown up in big cities. Some of them have hardly ever been to a wood or a field, and they can be quite frightened at first, of insects, or of getting dirty. Jack: But schools usually provide boots and coats, don't they? Priya: Yes, clothing isn't really the problem. It's more about helping them feel comfortable in a new environment. Jack: Did you do much outdoor learning at primary school yourself? Priya: Not much. But we had one teacher, Mr Hughes, who took us out to the woods every Friday, whatever the weather. I'm still really thankful to him. I remember everything we did there. Jack: It's funny, I had a teacher like that too. She's probably the reason I want to teach. I feel very grateful that she made the effort. Priya: We should mention that in the introduction. Shall we meet again on Thursday to put it all together? Jack: Sounds good. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about bats and rice farming in Thailand. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Good morning. Over the last few weeks, we've been looking at ecosystem services, that is, the benefits that people receive from wild species, often without realising it. Today I'd like to focus on a group of animals with a rather poor reputation: bats. Bats are often associated with darkness and disease, and many people find them frightening. But for farming communities living near their roosts, they can be extremely valuable neighbours, as I hope to show you today. I'll be drawing on a research project I took part in recently in a rice-growing province of central Thailand, where several large colonies of bats roost in limestone caves close to farmland. Lecturer: Most people in the area are small-scale rice farmers, and the bats bring them a surprising number of benefits. The species we studied feed at night on flying insects, and a large colony can eat several tonnes of them in a single night. People often assume that bats mainly eat mosquitoes, but we found relatively few of those. When we examined the bats' droppings, we found the remains of moths in large quantities, as well as planthoppers, tiny insects that can destroy entire rice fields. By reducing the numbers of these pests, the bats save farmers a great deal of money that would otherwise be spent on chemicals. Lecturer: The droppings themselves are valuable too. They're known as guano, and local people collect them from the cave floors and sell them. In the past, guano was also used to make gunpowder, but today it's used almost entirely as a fertiliser, because it's so rich in nutrients. Farmers told us it gave better results than anything they could buy in a shop. Lecturer: Other species of bat feed on nectar rather than insects, and they're important pollinators. It's sometimes said that mangoes depend on bats, but in fact they're mainly pollinated by insects. The durian, on the other hand, is a very good example. Its flowers open at night, and bats are its main pollinators, so without them, farmers would harvest far less of this valuable fruit. Lecturer: In recent years, the bats have also brought income of another kind. Every evening, just at dusk, millions of bats pour out of the caves in long, twisting streams, and this spectacle now attracts large numbers of tourists, who spend money in local restaurants and guesthouses. The bats return at dawn, but very few visitors get up early enough to see that. Lecturer: However, despite these benefits, bat numbers in the region appear to be falling, and our project looked at the reasons. Over two years, we interviewed more than two hundred households and also counted the bats leaving several caves at regular intervals. One important cause is disturbance in the caves. Guano collection is a valuable source of income, but when collectors enter the caves during the breeding season, mothers may abandon or drop their young. The authorities have tried to ban collection during those months, but the rules aren't always followed. Lecturer: Bats are also hunted in some areas. Before we started, I'd assumed they were caught mainly for use in traditional medicine, but the people we spoke to told us it was for their meat, which is sold at local markets. That's a concern for human health as well, as bats can carry viruses. Lecturer: Loss of roosting sites is another problem. Some species roost in temples, where they're generally left alone. But others live in hollow trees, and as old trees have been cut down to make way for farmland and roads, these bats have lost their homes. And finally, noise from traffic seemed to make little difference to the bats, but we found that bright lighting near cave entrances, from new roads and tourist facilities, delayed their emergence in the evening, which meant they had less time to feed. Lecturer: So what can be done? We considered planting more trees, but that would take decades to have any effect. Instead, we tested the installation of bat boxes. These are small wooden shelters fixed to poles near the rice fields, and within a year, around half of them were being used. We also found that bats were more numerous on farms where farmers had reduced the amount of pesticides they used. These chemicals not only kill the insects that bats feed on, but may also poison the bats themselves. Persuading farmers to change their habits isn't easy, of course, so in the second part of the lecture, I'll look at how we tried to do that. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
